newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Gujral says too early to recognise Taleban.
newsitem.headline: India's Gujral says too early to recognise Taleban.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said on Monday it was too early for New Delhi to decide whether it would recognise the Taleban as the legitimate government of Afghanistan.

Asked whether India would recognise the Taleban government, Gujral told Asian News International in an interview: "There is no settled government right now so there is no question of our changing recognition right now."

After the Taleban Islamic militia won major victories in northern Afghanistan last month, it won diplomatic recognition from Pakistan. The Indian Foreign Ministry last week said it was watching the situation carefully.
Opposition forces have since started closing in on the Taleban in the north, and driven them out of the northern capital of Mazar-i-Sharif.
Asked about the Taleban's attempts to seize control of the nation, Gujral said: "India basically has always felt and continues to feel that all these matters are internal affairs of Afghanistan.
"We do feel unhappy that the Afghan people have suffered for more than two to three decades now and we would be happy if this era of agony for the people of Afghanistan ends."
India has repeatedly called for an end to foreign interference in Afghanistan and accused arch-foe Pakistan of aiding Taleban warriors. Pakistan says it is neutral.

"Ultimately, the issues have to be sorted out by the Afghan people themselves, and from that point of view it has been our approach and outlook that outside powers in countries should not intervene or interfere or support one faction or the other," Gujral said.
Since the Taleban swept into Kabul last September, New Delhi has expressed concern over the rise of religious fundamentalism in Central Asia.

The Taleban have frequently accused India, along with Russia and Iran, of supporting the forces of ousted Afghan President Burhanuddin Rabbani, who was driven from Kabul last September when the Taleban took the city.
The Taleban criticised India in April when it hosted a ministerial meeting of the Non-Aligned Movement to which a representative of Rabbani's ousted government was invited.
The widow of former Afghan president Najibullah, who was hanged by the Taleban after they seized Kabul, lives in Delhi with family members.
